title: 300,000-year-old tools found exactly where they fell in portugal
dek: Archaeologists uncovered more than 200 stone artefacts in their original context, pushing back the timeline of human presence in western Iberia.
body: More than 200 stone artefacts lie exactly where prehistoric people left them, buried at Vale do Forno near Alpiarça in central Portugal. The site, investigated since 2024, pushes human activity in western Iberia back to the Middle Pleistocene, more than 300,000 years ago. João Ribeiro of the University of Lisbon says this represents the earliest known evidence of sustained human occupation in the region.

The discovery matters because finding artefacts in their original depositional context is rare. Carlos Ferreira, also from the University of Lisbon, explained that the tools were found exactly where prehistoric man left them, untouched by later movement or geological processes. This intact context allows researchers to study spatial relationships between objects and surrounding deposits, something often lost at other Palaeolithic sites in Portugal and Spain.

Stone artefacts were first identified in the area during the 1990s, but archaeologists did not initially recognise the extent of the surviving deposits. More recent work has demonstrated that the site contains a substantial assemblage of prehistoric stone tools in unusually good condition. The preservation distinguishes Vale do Forno from many other known sites, offering a rare glimpse of a landscape shaped by early humans.

The age of the assemblage places the occupation within a period associated with significant developments in hominin populations and stone-tool technologies across Europe. However, the researchers have not yet identified which hominin population was responsible for the activity at Vale do Forno. No human fossils have been recovered from the site so far.

Further analysis will focus on the stone artefacts and associated archaeological deposits. Researchers also hope to recover genetic material from ancient animal remains found at the location. Such evidence could help reconstruct the environment inhabited by the prehistoric population and identify animal species living in central Portugal during the period of occupation.

The team hopes to recover ancient DNA to understand which species accompanied prehistoric humans in what is now Portugal. Continued investigation could therefore provide important evidence for understanding the chronology and character of early human occupation along the western edge of the Iberian Peninsula. The site sits on the western fringe of the peninsula, a route likely used by moving populations.

Vale do Forno joins a growing list of sites that are rewriting the story of human dispersal into Europe. Because the tools were found in situ, the dating and context are unusually reliable for this time depth. doesnt_show: The study does not yet identify which hominin species made the tools, nor does it provide a detailed reconstruction of the daily life or subsistence strategies of the occupants.
settle: Recovering human fossils or ancient DNA from the site would confirm who made the tools and how they related to other Eurasian populations.
